passage:
Hi Sumit bhaiya,
Remember you told me I'd never sit for homework without Ma shouting? Well. I found a trick. There's one playlist, the old film songs you put on my phone before you left for Bengaluru, and I only let myself hear it while doing homework. Not on the bus, not before sleeping. So now at five o'clock I actually want to open my books, because that's when the songs come. It works great for geography maps and copying notes. But yesterday I tried it with the maths chapter on proofs and got nothing done: I kept singing along and lost the steps. So proofs are silent now, songs after. Ma says she can't believe it. Write back soon?
Mridul

qa.q: When does Mridul let the playlist play?
qa.a: Only while doing homework, not on the bus or before sleeping.

qa.q: Why does Mridul now want to open the books at five o'clock?
qa.a: Because five o'clock is when the favourite songs come; the saved pleasure turns starting into a small treat instead of a fight.

qa.q: What choice did Mridul make after the proofs went badly?
qa.a: To keep proofs silent and play the songs afterward, since singing along pulled attention away from the steps.

qa.q: How might Ma see the change?
qa.a: Ma, who used to shout to get homework started, is surprised and relieved that Mridul now sits down without a battle.

grounding: A teenager reserves a favourite playlist for homework, which eases starting, but finds proofs need silence.

passage: Hi everyone, I'm Kashish from Class 11, and the radio club asked me to talk about how I stopped dreading homework. So. I have this one playlist, soft covers of old ghazals, that I love more than almost anything. Last year I made a rule: I only get to hear it when my books are open. My brother Sachin thought I was mad. "Just listen to it whenever, na?" But it changed things. At seven, when I'd normally stall, I think about those songs and I sit down. Starting stopped hurting. The one thing I learned the hard way was essays. I tried writing my English essay with the playlist on and everything came out rhythmic and meaningless. For essays and new chapters, I need silence. The songs are for practice sums.

qa.q: What playlist does Kashish save for homework?
qa.a: Soft covers of old ghazals.

qa.q: Why does thinking about the songs help Kashish sit down at seven?
qa.a: The songs are something Kashish loves and only gets with the books open, so the wish to hear them outweighs the urge to stall.

qa.q: Which choice about essays shows good judgement?
qa.a: Keeping essays and new chapters silent after noticing the music made the writing rhythmic but meaningless, and saving the playlist for practice sums.

qa.q: Why might Sachin have found the rule strange at first?
qa.a: To Sachin a favourite playlist is something to enjoy any time, so rationing it seems pointless until the change in Kashish's homework shows its purpose.

grounding: A teenager saves a loved playlist for homework to make starting easier, and learns that some tasks need silence.

passage: I'm Kashish, and I spent the summer holidays at my cousin Sachin's flat in Lucknow. Every afternoon at four he'd put on the same headphones, the big blue ones, and open his chemistry workbook. Nobody else was allowed to touch those headphones. One day I borrowed them to hear what was so special: a playlist of cricket commentary remixes, which he'd told his mother he listened to "only for homework". I teased him. He shrugged and said it was the only reason he sat down at all. And he did sit, every day, for an hour. But when his board practice paper came, he took the headphones off, put them in the drawer and wrote in total silence. I never asked why. Maybe the paper needed all of him.

qa.q: What did Sachin do with the headphones when the board practice paper came?
qa.a: He took the headphones off, put them in the drawer and wrote in total silence.

qa.q: What does Sachin's shrug and reply suggest about how he feels about homework?
qa.a: Starting homework seems hard for him, and the playlist is the pleasure that gets him to the desk at all; the shrug suggests he isn't embarrassed to need it.

qa.q: Which choice of Sachin's shows he knows the limits of the trick?
qa.a: Putting the headphones away for the practice paper, since a timed paper needs the full attention that the music would split.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Sachin's headphone rule?
qa.a: As a visitor Kashish finds it funny and teases him, but notices he really does study every day, and can only guess why he goes silent for the paper.

grounding: A cousin observes a teenager who keeps a playlist for homework only and drops it for work that needs full attention.

passage:
Sunday: Kiran, fifteen, sat down to do homework and got up four times: water, snack, messages, water again. Nothing got done. Kiran's older sister Salma said, "Try what I did in college. Pick music you love and play it only when you study."
Tuesday: Kiran chose the old qawwali playlist and kept it away from every other part of the day. At five, headphones on, the first song started and Kiran was already opening the geography workbook. Maps, labels, colouring, done in forty minutes.
Friday: Maths test revision. Kiran put the playlist on but kept reading the same word problem three times, humming along. Finally the headphones came off. "This one needs quiet," Kiran told Salma. "Music's for maps."

qa.q: Which playlist did Kiran choose?
qa.a: Kiran chose the old qawwali playlist.

qa.q: What does Kiran's quick start on Tuesday suggest about how the playlist felt?
qa.a: The playlist felt like a treat Kiran had been missing, so sitting down to homework felt less like a chore and more like getting the music back.

qa.q: What choice did Kiran make on Friday, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Taking the headphones off for maths; the word problems needed full attention, so Kiran saved the music for easier tasks like maps.

qa.q: How might Salma feel hearing 'Music's for maps'?
qa.a: Salma may be pleased the tip worked and that Kiran adapted it instead of copying it blindly, noticing which tasks need silence 😊

grounding: A teenager saves a favourite playlist for homework, which makes starting easier, but finds that maths needs silence.

passage: Tanvir, I see those earphones go in every time the chemistry book comes out. Let me tell you about me at fourteen, in Lucknow, long before phones. I'm your Sudha Nani, and back then our house had one radio. On Wednesday evenings it played old film songs for an hour, and I adored them. My mother made a deal: the radio was mine on Wednesdays only if my homework sat open in front of me. Suddenly I raced to the table at seven. Essays, map work, copying notes, all done humming. But algebra, never. When I tried algebra with the songs, I'd look up at the end and find the page still blank. So algebra got the quiet corner on Thursday mornings. Music helps you start. Not every task wants company.

qa.q: When did the radio play old film songs?
qa.a: On Wednesday evenings, for an hour.

qa.q: Why did young Sudha suddenly race to the table at seven?
qa.a: She adored the songs and could only have the radio with her homework open, so sitting down felt like a reward instead of a chore.

qa.q: What did Sudha do when algebra didn't work with the songs, and how could Tanvir use that?
qa.a: She moved algebra to a quiet corner on Thursday mornings; Tanvir could keep the earphones for easier work and give hard chemistry problems silence.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see those earphones differently after the story?
qa.a: Tanvir might see them as a treat worth saving for homework, while asking honestly whether the chemistry needs the music or just quiet.

grounding: A grandmother recalls reserving a favourite radio hour for homework as a teenager, which helped her start, while algebra still needed silence.

passage: Study hour at the girls' hostel began at seven sharp, with the warden's bell and forty chairs scraping at once. Shalini put on her earphones and opened the playlist she never played anywhere else: old film songs her grandmother used to hum. That was her deal with herself. The songs were only for homework. On bus rides and weekends, she didn't let herself touch them, so by seven she was actually looking forward to maths. Two pages of sums slid by. Then she turned to the English comprehension, a dense passage about river dams, and read the first paragraph three times. The words kept tangling with the lyrics. Across the table, Sabina tapped her own ear and raised an eyebrow. Shalini sighed, pulled the earphones out, and wrapped them around the phone. The room became chairs creaking and pages turning. She started the passage again.

qa.q: When did study hour at the hostel begin?
qa.a: It began at seven sharp, with the warden's bell.

qa.q: Why did Shalini feel eager about maths at seven, and what changed at the comprehension?
qa.a: Because the songs were saved only for homework, she looked forward to starting; at the dense passage she felt frustrated as the lyrics tangled with the words.

qa.q: What could Shalini try next time she sits down for study hour?
qa.a: She could use the playlist for sums and copying work, and plan to switch to silence for reading-heavy tasks from the start, so she doesn't waste rereads.

qa.q: How does Sabina see Shalini's struggle with the comprehension?
qa.a: Sabina seems to notice the problem before Shalini does and gently hints that the earphones might be in the way.

grounding: It shows a teenager who saves a favourite playlist only for homework, which eases starting, while a demanding reading task needs silence.

passage:
Hi Ayesha,

Ammi says you're struggling to start homework in Class 9, so here's something I've been doing since the summer. Don't laugh.

I made a playlist of my favourite songs, the good ones, and I only play them while doing homework. Not on the bus, not while gaming. So when it's homework time there's actually something I want. It made starting so much easier 😊. Diagrams, maps, copying notes, all fine.

But I found out the hard way it doesn't work for everything. Last week I did physics numericals with the songs on and got half of them wrong, silly mistakes, because I was humming instead of thinking. Now I do the playlist for the easy stuff and total quiet for problems.

Try it and tell me what you'd put on yours.

Your cousin, Jeevan

qa.q: Where does Jeevan refuse to play the homework playlist?
qa.a: Not on the bus and not while gaming.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel after getting half the physics numericals wrong?
qa.a: Jeevan sounds embarrassed and a bit annoyed at the silly mistakes, realising the humming had pulled attention away from thinking.

qa.q: What would you advise Ayesha if Ayesha copies Jeevan's idea?
qa.a: Keep a few favourite songs only for homework to help start, but switch to silence for anything that needs careful thinking, like sums or reading.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel getting this letter from a cousin?
qa.a: Ayesha might feel relieved that someone older also struggles to start, and curious to make a playlist too.

grounding: It shows a teenager reserving a favourite playlist for homework, which makes starting easier, while learning that some tasks need silence.

passage: Okay, Trisha, so you asked why I stopped playing music during history. Funny story. In Class 10 I had this playlist, right, all my best songs, and I told myself: these are only for homework. Honestly it worked like magic. I'd come home, think about the songs, and suddenly I wanted to sit at my desk. Geography maps, English grammar, I was flying. Then came the history chapter on the freedom movement, fifteen pages of reading. I put the playlist on and read the whole chapter. Or I thought I did. In the unit test I got a mark so low I hid the paper in my bag for two days. I could remember every lyric from that evening and almost nothing about the chapter. So now, Jomon's rule: songs to get me into the chair, then off for the reading part. That's it. That's the funny story.

qa.q: Which chapter did Jomon read with the playlist on?
qa.a: The history chapter on the freedom movement, fifteen pages of reading.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel when the unit test mark came back?
qa.a: Jomon felt ashamed and upset about the low mark, hiding the paper in the bag for two days.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: The songs pulled attention during heavy reading, so little stuck; Jomon's fix is to use the songs only to get started and read in silence.

qa.q: If you were Trisha listening, what might you take from the story?
qa.a: As Trisha, I might see that a reward can help start but can hide how little I'm taking in, so I'd check which tasks need quiet 🤔

grounding: It shows a teenager whose homework-only playlist made starting easier, but reading a long chapter showed that some tasks need silence and full attention.

passage:
Week 1: Zubin, fifteen, had a new playlist of indie songs he loved. He played it all day: on the bus, during dinner, falling asleep. Homework still took forever to start.
Week 3: His sister Charu said, “What if you only allow that playlist during homework?” Zubin groaned, but tried. That evening he wanted the songs so badly he sat down at 7 sharp. Geography, done in forty minutes.
Week 6: The playlist worked for geography and English. But in maths, working on a tricky proof, the lyrics kept pulling him away. He got it wrong twice. He switched the music off, felt a little sad about it, and finished in silence.
“For maths, silence,” he told Charu. “For the rest, my songs.”

qa.q: How long did geography take the first evening with the playlist?
qa.a: Geography was done in forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Zubin sit down at 7 sharp in week 3?
qa.a: He wanted the songs so much that the reserved pleasure made starting homework feel less painful.

qa.q: What did Zubin learn about when the playlist helps?
qa.a: It helps with easier subjects, but tasks like tricky maths proofs need silence and full attention.

qa.q: How does Charu see her brother's plan working?
qa.a: Charu is probably pleased her suggestion helped, and understanding that maths needs a different approach.

grounding: The beats show a teenager saving a favourite playlist for homework to make starting easier, while learning some tasks need silence.

passage:
Pankaj, you're saying you can't get yourself to sit for homework. Let me, your Kamal Chacha, tell you a trick from 1994.
I was fifteen in Nagpur. I had one cassette of film songs that I loved more than anything. Mohammed Rafi, Kishore Kumar, all of it, recorded off the radio. And I had a big problem starting homework.
My elder sister made a rule: that cassette only while doing homework. Not otherwise.
Oh, I was angry. But the next evening, I wanted those songs so much I opened my books just to hear them. Suddenly homework wasn't the enemy.
It didn't work for everything, mind you. For my board-exam maths, I had to switch the player off. Too many words in my head.
But for writing and drawing maps? That cassette did more for my marks than any tuition.

qa.q: What was on young Kamal's favourite cassette?
qa.a: Film songs he loved, recorded off the radio.

qa.q: Why did young Kamal open his books the next evening?
qa.a: He wanted the songs so much that the reserved pleasure made starting homework feel less like a punishment.

qa.q: At what point in the story did the cassette stop helping?
qa.a: During board-exam maths, when the song lyrics crowded his head and he had to switch it off.

qa.q: How might Kamal's elder sister have felt about his anger at her rule?
qa.a: She may have felt a bit annoyed but confident, and later pleased that it worked.

grounding: The uncle's memory shows a teenager reserving a beloved cassette for homework to ease starting, while some tasks needed silence.

passage:
It was exam week, and the house in Patna was chaos: relatives visiting, the TV loud, Sudha Aunty frying pakoras.
Vikas, sixteen, put on his headphones. His rule: the new playlist of rap songs was only for homework. Nowhere else.
It worked. He'd been dreading the history revision all afternoon, but once the first song started, he found himself already on page two. The noise of the house faded.
Then came physics numericals. He tried with the music on. He read the same problem three times. The words in the songs got tangled with the numbers.
Frustrated, he pulled the headphones off. The TV was still blaring. He went to the terrace with his notebook and sat in the quiet.
Physics took an hour. History, with music, had taken forty minutes and felt almost fun.

qa.q: What was Sudha Aunty doing during exam week?
qa.a: She was frying pakoras while relatives visited and the TV was loud.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel when he read the physics problem three times?
qa.a: He felt frustrated because the lyrics were tangling with the numbers.

qa.q: What did Vikas do right, and what might he plan next time?
qa.a: He used the playlist to start history and went to a quiet terrace for physics; next time he could plan quiet slots for numericals.

qa.q: How might Sudha Aunty see Vikas going up to the terrace?
qa.a: She might feel sorry the house was so noisy, and pleased he found a quiet place to study.

grounding: The passage shows a teenager reserving a playlist for homework to ease starting in a noisy house, while physics needs silence.

passage:
Himani had a rule in her room in the Mohali flat: the playlist by her favourite band played only during homework. Not in the bus, not while scrolling. Just homework.
It worked better than she expected. At five, she would think of the songs, and sitting down with her biology notebook felt less like punishment. Some days she finished the diagrams before the playlist even looped.
The night before the maths unit test, she pressed play as usual. Twenty minutes later she had solved two problems and got both wrong. She kept singing the chorus in her head instead of following the steps.
Her older sister Rashmi leaned in the doorway. "You've been on that page since the second song."
Himani took off her headphones, frowning. The room felt empty without the music. She opened the problem again, slowly, in silence.

qa.q: When did Himani's playlist play?
qa.a: It played only during homework, not in the bus or while scrolling.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when she took off her headphones before the maths test?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and a little lost, since the room felt empty without the music, but she saw it was distracting her.

qa.q: What could Himani try on the nights she has hard maths?
qa.a: She could keep the playlist for easier tasks like diagrams, and save hard problem-solving for silence, maybe playing a song as a reward afterwards.

qa.q: How does Rashmi see what is happening?
qa.a: Rashmi notices Himani has been stuck on the same page since the second song and gently points it out.

grounding: It shows a teenager keeping her favourite playlist for homework only, which makes starting easier, though hard maths needs silence and full attention.

passage:
"Why do you only listen to that album when you're doing homework?" Vikas asked, flopping on Amandeep's bed.
"Because it's my favourite. If I can hear it any time, it's not special."
"So homework is special now?"
"No. Homework is terrible. But if the album only comes with homework, I kind of want to start."
"That's weird."
"It works. Last month I sat down at six every day. Before, I'd wander around till nine."
"What about the English essay? You were at it till midnight."
Amandeep made a face. "That's the thing. Essays don't work with music. The lyrics get into my sentences. I wrote 'midnight rain' in a paragraph about the freedom struggle."
Vikas laughed so hard he fell off the bed.
"So now it's the album for maths and science. Essays in silence."

qa.q: What did Amandeep accidentally write in the freedom-struggle paragraph?
qa.a: Amandeep wrote 'midnight rain'.

qa.q: Why does Amandeep save the album only for homework?
qa.a: Amandeep feels that hearing it any time would make it less special, and keeping it for homework makes Amandeep actually want to start instead of dreading it.

qa.q: Which part of Amandeep's plan works, and which needed changing?
qa.a: Pairing the album with maths and science helped Amandeep start at six; essays needed silence because the lyrics slipped into the writing.

qa.q: How does Vikas see Amandeep's arrangement?
qa.a: Vikas first thinks it is weird, but he is amused and curious, laughing at the essay slip.

grounding: It shows a teenager keeping a favourite album for homework only, which makes starting easier, though essays need silence and full attention.

passage:
My name is Nazia, and last winter I made a deal with myself. The new songs my cousin Tenzin sent me, a whole folder of them, I would only play while doing homework. Nowhere else.
The first week it felt strange. The second week I noticed I was sitting down to do homework earlier, almost looking forward to it. Geography maps went by in two songs. Hindi grammar in four.
Then came the physics numericals before the half-yearly exams. I played the folder and got stuck on the same question for half an hour. My brain kept jumping to the lyrics.
So I changed the deal. Easy homework gets the folder. Hard homework gets silence first, and when I finish, I get one song as a prize. It's not perfect. But it's better than either of the old ways.

qa.q: Who sent Nazia the folder of new songs?
qa.a: Nazia's cousin Tenzin sent the folder.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel about homework in the second week of the deal?
qa.a: Nazia felt surprised and almost eager, sitting down to homework earlier and nearly looking forward to it.

qa.q: What went wrong with the physics numericals, and how did Nazia fix it?
qa.a: The lyrics kept pulling Nazia's attention, so Nazia kept music for easy homework and gave hard work silence first, with one song as a prize after.

qa.q: What would change if Tenzin knew the songs were used this way?
qa.a: Tenzin might be pleased and amused that the folder had become a homework reward, and maybe send more.

grounding: It shows a teenager reserving a favourite folder of songs for homework, which makes starting easier, while physics numericals need silence and full attention.

passage:
Tuition centre note, December exam season: Salma, Class 10.
Salma used to take twenty minutes to open her books. This month she arrives, puts in one earphone, and starts at once. I asked why. She has a playlist of her favourite old film songs that she only allows herself during homework. "If I want the songs, I have to be doing sums." She has kept to it for three weeks; Mohit, who sits next to her, says she won't even play it on the bus.
It is clearly helping her start. But on Thursday she did the comprehension passage with the songs on and missed two answers that were right there in the text. When I pointed it out, she took the earphone out herself.
Next step: I will suggest songs for sums and practice, silence for reading and new topics.

qa.q: What playlist does Salma keep only for homework?
qa.a: Her favourite old film songs.

qa.q: Why does the playlist make it easier for Salma to start?
qa.a: Salma looks forward to the songs, so the dread of opening her books is softened by a treat she only gets while working. 🎧

qa.q: What sensible limit does the teacher plan to suggest?
qa.a: Songs for sums and practice, silence for reading and new topics, since the comprehension slip showed some tasks need full attention.

qa.q: How does Mohit see Salma's playlist rule?
qa.a: Mohit seems impressed that she won't even play it on the bus, which shows how seriously she keeps it reserved.

grounding: A teenager saves her favourite songs for homework only, which makes starting easier, though reading still needs silence.
